en.content:
The reopening of the Hong Kong Museum of History’s flagship “Hong Kong Story” after a six-year revamp marks a defining moment for the city’s cultural landscape. A permanent exhibition that foregrounds the shared historical roots between the city and the mainland reflects a broader, official aim to situate Hong Kong within the national narrative while modernising the way history is presented to the public. This is timely: generations who grew up in a rapidly globalising city need accessible, curated accounts of origins, institutions and turning points to make sense of their place in a changing China and an interconnected world.

That said, the curatorship of such a major civic institution carries responsibilities beyond celebratory framing. History museums earn public trust by balancing narrative coherence with evidentiary rigor, welcoming diverse perspectives and acknowledging complexities. The new Hong Kong Story has the opportunity to model this balance — by foregrounding archival research, facilitating dialogue with local scholars and educators, and offering interpretive layers that allow visitors to explore multiple facets of the city’s past. Doing so will help the exhibition speak not only to civic identity and national belonging, but also to the curiosity and critical thinking of younger audiences.

Finally, the museum’s relaunch should be seen as an invitation to civic engagement rather than a closed declaration. Outreach programmes, school partnerships and bilingual interpretive materials will be essential to ensure the exhibition resonates across communities and contributes to social cohesion. In combining a confident presentation of shared roots with open, scholarly stewardship, the Hong Kong Museum of History can strengthen cultural confidence, enrich public knowledge, and support the city’s ongoing role as a bridge between local distinctiveness and the broader national narrative.
